title: Retire the historical planning documents in docs/plans
description:
`docs/plans/` holds four documents totalling ~2,500 lines. Three of them describe work that has since landed, and the convention now is that plans are working artifacts that get deleted once the work is done rather than kept as standing design documents.

They are also the only part of the tree exempted from `scripts/lint_process_labels.py`, because they are dense with bead IDs, PR references and time-state wording. Retiring them narrows or removes that exemption.

## The four

`extract-from-experiments.md` (159 lines) — a one-off migration plan for pulling experimental code out of `../learn/z3950`. The migration happened. Nothing references it.

`implementation-plan.md` (947 lines) — a phased handoff written for an implementation team that turned out to be one person. Its phases are built.

`app-plan.md` (364 lines) — the original application plan. Largely implemented; whatever design rationale in it is still live belongs in `docs/` proper or in a bead, not in a plan.

`long-term-plan.md` (1,027 lines) — different from the other three. It is a July 2026 review plus a forward plan, written deliberately and merged recently, and it is the only one describing work that has not happened yet.

## Shape

For the first three: confirm nothing in `docs/` or the README links to them, extract any design rationale that is still true and not recorded elsewhere, then delete them. Git history keeps them.

`long-term-plan.md` needs a decision rather than a default. Either it stays as the living roadmap — in which case the lint exemption stays for that one file and it should be kept current — or its forward-looking content becomes beads and the file goes. The second is more consistent with tracking work in one place, but it is a real loss of narrative that beads do not carry well.

Once the directory is empty or down to one file, tighten `EXCLUDED_PATHS` in `scripts/lint_process_labels.py` accordingly.

title: Review queue visibility for non-staff catalogers
description:
`review_queue` in `ingest/views.py` filters pending scans to `scanned_by=request.user` unless the user is staff, and `confirm_scan`, `discard_scan` and the title-page endpoints apply the same rule. The workflow the project describes, several people scanning while one reviews, works only when the reviewer holds the staff flag, which also grants the admin. bd-nzb carries the same scoping into the queue count on the mode bar, so the decision affects a second surface.

Decide between: every logged-in cataloger sees and can act on the whole pending queue (drop the filter; a queue for a circle of friends does not need per-user privacy); or a reviewer role separate from staff (a Django group and a permission check in place of `is_staff`). The first is a two-line change plus tests; the second is the shape a multi-catalog server would need. Record the decision here and apply it to every view that checks `scanned_by`.

title: cleanup_staging sweeps tmp/title_pages while staged images live under media/staging
description:
`ingest/management/commands/cleanup_staging.py` deletes `discarded` ScanResults older than the retention period, then removes old files from `BASE_DIR/tmp/title_pages/`. That directory was the staging area before the title-page handoff; uploads go to `ScanResult.image` under `MEDIA_ROOT/staging/YYYY/MM/DD/` (`staging_image_path` in `ingest/models.py`), so the orphan sweep reads a directory nothing writes to.

Point the sweep at `MEDIA_ROOT/staging/` and define an orphan as a file no ScanResult references that is older than the retention period. Deleting a ScanResult row through the ORM does not delete its file, so delete `scan.image` on the rows the command removes as well; discarding a title scan already deletes the file at discard time, so this covers rows discarded by other paths and files whose delete failed.

otzar-eiy proposes a separate command for stale `awaiting_ocr` rows. Fold it in here as a second criterion with its own threshold rather than adding a second janitor. Update the `cleanup_staging` section of the administration guide.

comments.author: dchud
comments.text: When rewriting the sweep, go through the storage API (default_storage.listdir and delete) rather than os.listdir: under bd-n7a media moves to S3 (bd-n7a.2), and a directory walk finds nothing there.

title: Rework the review queue into scannable rows with inline confirm
description:
The queue shows a candidate count and hides everything else behind a
Details button at the far right of each row. Deciding whether a scan
matched the right book means clicking through, and the expanded view
then offers "Use this" with little more to go on.

`_candidates.html` -- written for the title-page cascade results --
already renders the layout this needs: title/author, date,
publisher/place, series, identifiers, source, one row per candidate.
The queue's `_queue_item.html` predates it and duplicates none of it.

## Shape

Extract the candidate row markup from `_candidates.html` into a shared
partial and render it in the queue, so both surfaces stay in step.

Clicking a row expands it in place (Alpine is already in this template)
to show the full field set the record would receive -- subjects,
additional authors, identifiers, language, series -- with a Confirm
button inside the expanded row, so the decision and the action sit
together.

Each row also carries a "See full record" link that POSTs the candidate
JSON to `select_candidate`, which already stores it in session and
redirects to `/ingest/confirm/`. That is the same review page the
title-page results reach, so the queue stops being the one path that
commits without a preview. No new view is needed.

## Zero-candidate scans

A scan with no candidates currently says so only behind Details. Those
rows should say it at the top level and offer an action -- re-run the
search, or discard -- rather than expanding into an empty box.

## Prerequisite, already landed

Both confirm paths now build records through
`_create_record_from_candidate` (commit 8b4b6ca), so the inline Confirm
and the review page produce identical records. That had to come first;
before it, the queue path silently dropped `source_marc` and any date
that would not parse as an integer.

## Testing

E2e for expand-in-place, inline Confirm, and See full record reaching
`/ingest/confirm/`. The record-equivalence unit tests already exist.

title: Image decode failure leaves the capture form dead and silent
description:
`_title_page_form.html` wraps `createImageBitmap` in a try/catch that
logs to the console and returns. The Upload button stays disabled and
the preview stays hidden.

The user taps "Take title page photo", picks an image, and nothing

title: Title-page scans never leave pending after a candidate is chosen
description:
Photograph a title page, run OCR, search catalogs, pick a candidate: a
Record is created and the ScanResult stays `status="pending"` with
`ocr_output` set, forever.

`title_page_poll` shows `pending` rows that have output, so the card
reappears in the "Incoming photos" pane on every device on every poll
tick, and sits in `/ingest/queue/` permanently. The pane fills with
scans that are already catalogued.

The link is dropped in the round trip. `_ocr_results.html`'s search form
posts only the metadata fields to `title_page_upload`; the response,
`_candidates.html`, has a "Use" button that posts to `select_candidate`
-> `confirm_candidate`. Nothing in that chain knows which ScanResult the
metadata came from, so nothing can mark it confirmed.

Carry `scan.id` through the search form and the candidate form, and set
`status="confirmed"`, `created_record`, and
`selected_candidate_index` when the record is created --
`confirm_scan` already does exactly this for the queue path.

Found in review of PR #7. P1 because every successful title-page ingest
leaves permanent debris in the one pane the workflow depends on.

title: Vendor HTMX and Alpine.js instead of loading them from unpkg
description:
`templates/base.html` loads HTMX 2.0.4 and Alpine.js 3.14.8 from unpkg.com. Every page that uses HTMX polling or Alpine state (the scan pages, the queue, dark mode, the ingest mode bar) depends on a third-party CDN being reachable from the browser, and cataloging happens at the shelves on whatever wifi is there. When the script fails to load, the page renders and the interactivity does not, with no error a user sees.

Copy the two files into `static/js/` with the version in each filename, reference them through `{% static %}` with the same `defer`, and let WhiteNoise serve them as it serves the stylesheet. Note the versions in the development guide so an upgrade is a file replacement. Add a test that no template references an external script host.

title: Stop embedding full candidate records in the results page
description:
`ingest/views.py` pairs each candidate with `json.dumps(c)` and `_candidates.html` writes that into a hidden `<textarea name="candidate_data">` on every row, so the entire candidate list — including everything the parser extracted — ships to the browser and comes back on submit.

Adding `source_marc` to parsed records grew this roughly ninefold: about 4.4 KB of MARC per candidate, taking a 20-candidate results page from 12.7 KB to 111 KB. An ISBN lookup hitting NLI, LC and DNB could reach roughly 300 KB. The page works, and this is not urgent, but the growth is structural: every field the parser learns to extract makes the page heavier, whether or not the browser needs it.

## Shape

The server already has what it needs. `ScanResult.candidate_records` holds the list and `confirm_scan` already selects by index, so the round trip could carry `(scan_id, candidate_index)` instead of the record itself, and `select_candidate` could read the candidate server-side rather than parsing it back out of the form.

The obstacle is that not every path into `_candidates.html` has a ScanResult to key off — check `isbn_lookup_view` and the title-page cascade search before assuming. If one path genuinely has no scan, that path can keep the embedded form and the common case can still be fixed.

Coordinate with bd-73m, which reworks the review queue and extracts a shared candidate row partial from this same template. Do this after that lands, not alongside it.

Compression (see the response-compression bead) reduces the symptom by about 85% and is a much smaller change; do that first and reassess whether this is still worth doing.

title: Edit multiple authors, publishers, locations and subjects in the manual entry form
description:
`RecordForm` in `ingest/forms.py` carries one author (name and romanized name), one publisher (name and place), one location, and no subject field. The models are many-to-many. A record with two authors or two shelf locations can be entered only through the admin, and subjects cannot be added or corrected outside the admin at all, which is where a cataloger ends up for every book with a translator or an editor. The same form serves `/ingest/edit/<id>/`, where `edit_record` shows only `record.authors.first()` and its siblings; check what the save path does with the relations the form cannot show before changing the form.

Turn the single fields into repeatable rows (Alpine for add and remove, a formset or a JSON list on the server side) for authors, publishers and locations, and add subjects with an autosuggest against existing headings in the style of the language field. Keep the authority check working per author row. E2e: enter a record with two authors and a subject, and see all of them on the record page and in search.

title: Decide which of ruff's newer default rules to adopt
description:
The dependency refresh pinned `[tool.ruff.lint] select`, which reproduces the rule set ruff 0.15.9 enabled by default. Without it the upgrade to 0.16.6 reported 89 findings across 24 files nobody had touched, because ruff's implicit default grew from 62 enabled rules to 416.

Pinning was the right call for a dependency PR — it keeps a linter upgrade from becoming a code-change PR — but it defers a decision rather than making one. The pin now states the project's rule set explicitly, which is an improvement regardless; the question is whether that set should stay where 0.15.9 happened to leave it.

## Already decided

`I` (isort) was adopted in the same PR and is not part of this decision. It was never in ruff's default set, so the pin did not drop it; enabling it ratified what the tree already did, and a canonical import order makes the merge conflicts parallel work produces in shared modules resolve mechanically. Seven files were fixed automatically.

## What remains: the 89 findings

Roughly 72 are `RUF012` (mutable class attributes should be annotated `ClassVar`), which lands almost entirely on Django model `Meta` and admin classes — arguably noise for this codebase, since Django's own idiom is a bare list.

The rest are a mixed handful worth looking at individually: `BLE001` (blind `except Exception`), `S112` (`try`/`except`/`continue`), `B017` (assert on bare exception), `TRY401` (redundant exception object in `logging.exception`). Several of those point at real habits in the ingest and sources code, where broad excepts around network calls are deliberate but not always narrowed as tightly as they could be.

## Shape

Go through the categories rather than the 89 individual findings, and decide per rule: adopt and fix, adopt with targeted `noqa`, or leave out of `select` with a comment saying why. Ending with an explicit list that says what this project checks for is the deliverable; a clean run under someone else's defaults is not.

Do this as its own change, not folded into other work — it touches many files shallowly and would drown a review.

title: Keep subject subdivisions and dedupe repeated headings
description:
The ingest confirm page shows the same subject twice.

`sources/marc.py:210-216` keeps only the first `$a` of each 650 field
and discards the subdivisions (`$v $x $y $z`), with no deduplication.
That produces visually identical entries two ways, both routine:

- Subdivided headings collapse. `650 _0 $a Jews $z Israel $x History.`
  and `650 _0 $a Jews $x Social life and customs.` both emit `Jews`.
- Parallel vocabularies repeat. LC records carry an LCSH `650 _0 $a
  Judaism.` alongside a FAST `650 _7 $a Judaism. $2 fast`; the `$2` is
  invisible here, so the list holds the heading twice.

Reproduced against a synthetic LC-shaped record: five 650 fields yielded
`['Jews', 'Jews', 'Judaism.', 'Judaism.', 'Jews']`.

The visible duplication is display-only -- `get_or_create(heading=...)`
collapses equal headings and the through table has a unique index, so no
duplicate rows exist. The real defect is underneath it: two distinct
headings are both stored as the broad subject `Jews`. The intended form
joins subdivisions with " -- ", as `load_test_data.py:284-289` shows
("Talmud -- Commentaries").

Fix by assembling the heading from `$a` plus subdivisions and deduping
on a normalized key, in `sources/marc.py`. `_attach_from_candidate` is
the single writer for all three ingest paths, so one fix covers
everything. Deduping in the template would hide the symptom and keep
storing the wrong subject.

Existing tests stay green (`tests/test_marc.py:282-284` covers 650s that
carry only `$a`). Add a case with a subdivided 650 plus a duplicate FAST
650, and an e2e assertion that the confirm page lists each subject once.

The 8 existing Subject rows were written under the truncating logic; a
backfill would need the original MARC, and no stored record has
`source_marc` populated yet.

title: Hard-wrap the user-facing docs at 79 columns
description:
`docs/administration.md`, `docs/development.md` and `docs/user-guide.md` are written with unwrapped paragraphs — 52, 59 and 39 lines over 79 columns respectively, some past 500 characters.

CLAUDE.md now distinguishes the two cases: text submitted through GitHub stays unwrapped, because a manual wrap there is lost and produces noisy diffs; Markdown files in the repository are hard-wrapped at 79 columns, because they are read in a terminal as often as in a browser and nothing there reflows a 500-character line. These three files predate that rule and do not follow it.

## Scope

The three files above only. `docs/plans/` is excluded — those are working documents rather than user-facing, and bd-1yg covers what happens to them.

## Do it when the queue is clear

This is a whitespace-only diff across three files, which conflicts with anything else editing them. `docs/administration.md` in particular has been touched by two separate pull requests today. Wait until nothing is open against these files rather than forcing a rebase onto whoever is mid-flight.

Reflow only. No rewording, no restructuring, no corrections — a whitespace commit that also changes prose is unreviewable, because the reviewer cannot tell which is which. Anything worth fixing in the content gets its own change.

Leave fenced code blocks, table rows and long URLs alone; none of those are broken to fit.

Worth checking afterwards whether the pre-commit hook or the process-label lint should enforce the column limit on `docs/*.md`, so this does not drift back. That is a judgement call, not a requirement of this ticket — a hard gate on prose width can be more annoying than the drift it prevents.

title: pytest-socket is installed but never activated
description:
`pytest-socket` is a declared dev dependency and does nothing. There is no `--disable-socket` in `addopts`, no `disable_socket()` in any conftest, and nothing else turns it on. Tests can open sockets freely.

Verified rather than inferred: a probe test that connects a TCP socket to a public address succeeds during a normal `pytest` run.

## Why it matters

The suite talks to three kinds of remote service in the code it exercises — the Anthropic API for OCR, the SRU catalogs at NLI, LC and DNB, and Open Library for covers. Every test of those paths mocks the client, so nothing reaches the network today. That holds by convention, not by enforcement: a test that forgets a patch, or patches the wrong name, makes a real call and passes.

The Anthropic case is the expensive one — a real vision call costs money per test run and would not obviously look wrong in CI. The catalog case is the rude one: the SRU clients sleep `SRU_REQUEST_DELAY` between requests precisely because these are other people's servers.

This also contradicts what the project has been telling itself. `docs/plans/long-term-plan.md` lists "pytest-socket blocks accidental live HTTP in tests" among the project's strengths, and it has never been true.

## Shape

Enable it, then find out what breaks. `addopts = ["--disable-socket"]` with `--allow-unix-socket` is the usual shape, since the database and the live-server fixture need local sockets.

Expect the e2e suite to need thought rather than a flag. Playwright drives a browser in a separate process, so `pytest-socket` does not constrain it either way — that is a separate hole, and `tests/e2e/test_asset_delivery.py` shows the pattern that does work: a fixture that aborts off-origin requests through the browser context and asserts none were attempted.

Where a test genuinely needs a socket, `@pytest.mark.enable_socket` marks it deliberately, which is the point: the exceptions become visible.

title: Show the queue on /ingest/ and its depth in the ingest mode bar
description:
`/ingest/` renders three cards -- Scan barcode, Photograph title page,
Enter manually -- that the ingest mode bar (commit 25f39b3) now carries
on every ingest page. The cards duplicate the bar directly above them,
and the only thing left that is unique to the page is a "Review queue"
link.

Two changes, one dependent on the other:

`/ingest/` renders the queue itself. The route choice is already in the
bar, so the landing page can show what is waiting rather than repeating
the navigation. `/ingest/queue/` keeps working and renders the same
view.

The mode bar gains a Queue item carrying the pending count. This is the
part that answers "did what I just scanned land?" -- right after a scan
the user is standing on `/ingest/scan/`, not on the landing page, so a
count that lives only on `/ingest/` still has to be gone looking for.
The count is per-user, matching the existing queue scoping (staff see
all).

Depends on bd-queue-rows-r91 for what the rows look like; this ticket is
about where the queue appears and how its depth is surfaced.

## Testing

E2e that `/ingest/` lists pending scans, that the bar shows a count that
tracks what is actually pending, and that the count is visible at phone
width.

title: Repair the corrupted title on the existing DNB record
description:
Record `otzar-e` has the title `\x98The\x9c Complete Piano Etudes`. U+0098 and U+009C are the MARC non-sorting delimiters DNB wraps around a leading article, and browsers render them as blank, so the title reads as though it has stray whitespace in it.

Stripping them at parse time stops new records carrying them, but does nothing for rows already written. This is the data repair for what is already stored.

Depends on bd-osc landing first, so the parser and the repair agree on what a clean value looks like.

## Shape

A one-off management command, or a data migration if the set is small enough to enumerate. Scan every text field on `Record`, `Author`, `Publisher` and `Subject` for C1 control characters rather than assuming only titles carry them — the delimiters are legal in any MARC field with a non-sorting portion, and only titles have been checked.

Report what was found before changing anything. The live catalog is small enough that the honest first step is counting the affected rows and fields.

The FTS index in `catalog/search.py` holds its own copy of the indexed text, so a repaired record has to be re-indexed or the old bytes stay searchable.

title: Search and browse quality: prefix matching, Hebrew prefixes, facets, related items
description:
Catalog search matches whole tokens only, the site navigation links to the search page instead of carrying a search box, results cannot be narrowed, and the record page relates items by author and series but not by subject. Each is a bounded change to `catalog/search.py`, the search views, or the record detail view; none needs a different search engine. FTS5 is adequate at a few thousand records and stays.

Children, in the order they matter: prefix matching, then Hebrew prefix particles, then the navigation search box, then same-subject related items, then facets once the catalog is large enough that narrowing a result list is a real need.

Browse views sort by Unicode code point, not language-aware collation. Hebrew sorts acceptably because of code-point order; Latin titles with diacritics can sort oddly. No ticket for that until a browse page is seen to be wrong.

title: Match word prefixes in catalog search
description:
`_sanitize_query` in `catalog/search.py` quotes every word, so the FTS5 MATCH expression requires whole-token matches: `Rambam` finds records containing that token, `Ramb` finds nothing. Typing part of a name or title is the common case at a search box. The user guide says "Partial words match", which is wrong; its own example is a whole word.

FTS5 supports prefix queries natively: `"ramb"*` matches any token starting with `ramb`. Append `*` to each quoted word, or to the last word only, and check ranking on the test dataset so an exact token still outranks a prefix hit. The table is created with the default tokenizer (`ensure_fts_table`), so confirm how Hebrew tokens with attached geresh, gershayim or maqaf split before relying on prefix semantics for them.

Correct the user guide passage. Unit tests for prefix hits and for exact-over-prefix ranking; e2e for a partial-word search reaching the expected record.

title: Strip Hebrew prefix particles at index and query time
description:
A search for ספר does not match a record whose title carries הספר, בספר or לספר. The tokenizer splits on whitespace and punctuation, and the attached prefix letters (ב, ה, ו, כ, ל, מ, ש) are part of the token. A reader searching for a Hebrew word expects the inflected forms to match; the user guide documents this as a known limitation.

Two bounded options, either applied at both index time and query time so they agree. Index each Hebrew token as written and again with plausible leading prefix letters stripped, so a plain query for the base form matches; this keeps the query builder unchanged at the cost of a slightly larger index. Or expand the query to OR the written form with each prefix-stripped form. Indexing the extra forms is simpler to reason about.

Stripping is lossy in both directions, since the first letter of a word can be a real prefix or part of the root. Treat this as recall, not precision: an extra match costs less than a miss. Touches the same function as the prefix-matching ticket; land them in either order.

title: Put a search box in the site navigation
description: The header in `templates/base.html` carries a link to `/search/`, so a search starts with a click, a page load, then typing. A search box in the navigation submits straight to the search view from any page. `search_views.py` already reads `q` from GET, so this is a form in the header plus layout at phone width, where the box has to fit beside the existing links or collapse behind the menu. Keep the 44px touch targets and the focus ring styling the header uses. E2e: submit a query from the home page header and land on results.

title: Show same-subject items on the record page
description:
`record_detail` in `catalog/views.py` relates a record to other works by the same authors and to sibling volumes in its series, and not to records sharing a subject heading. For a collection where subjects are the organizing vocabulary (a tractate, a halakhic topic, commentaries on one book), same-subject items are the most useful related list after series siblings, and they are one query: records sharing any subject with this one, excluding itself, ordered by the number of shared subjects.

Cap the list as the author list is capped and render it under the same heading style. "Shelved nearby" (records at adjacent locations) is a separate idea that needs an ordering over `Location` labels, which are free text; it stays out of scope until locations are assigned consistently enough to sort.

title: Filter search results by language, decade and location
description:
Search results are one ranked list with no way to narrow them. Facets for language (the stored code, shown through `language_name`), publication decade (from `date_of_publication`), and location map directly onto fields the record carries, and the browse views already group by decade and by location.

Not needed while the catalog holds a few dozen records; a query that returns eight results does not need narrowing. The trigger is a search that regularly returns more than one screen. Implementation: fetch the FTS hit list, then filter the `Record` queryset by the chosen facet values, since FTS5 ranks and the ORM filters; per-value counts come from the filtered queryset.

title: Render language codes as language names
description:
Language shows as the raw code -- `heb` rather than `Hebrew` -- on the
record detail page, the ingest confirm page, the scan poll partial, the
manual entry form, and in the admin filter.

## The trap

MARC 008/35-37 carries ISO 639-2/**B** bibliographic codes, so German is
`ger`, not `deu`. `sources/marc.py:197` reads exactly those bytes, and
`catalog/language_views.py:19` already stores the bibliographic form.

`pycountry` (already a dependency) indexes ISO 639-3, where these exist
only as a `bibliographic` alias:

    pycountry.languages.get(alpha_3="ger")       -> None
    pycountry.languages.get(bibliographic="ger") -> German

An alpha_3-only lookup renders German, French, Dutch, Greek, Czech,
Persian, Chinese, Romanian, Welsh, Basque, Armenian, Icelandic,
Georgian, Macedonian, Maori, Malay, Burmese, Slovak, Albanian and
Tibetan as blank -- 20 divergences. Bibliographic lookup must come
first.

## Shape

A plain module `catalog/language_codes.py` plus a template filter
library, following the existing `bidi` templatetag pattern. Shared
rather than living inside the templatetag because
`catalog/language_views.py` is a second consumer.

Two display sites render plain dicts from session/JSON rather than model
instances, so this has to be a filter, not a model property.

A small override table is needed for MARC codes withdrawn from ISO 639-2
that ISO 639-3 has since reassigned -- `gae` means Scottish Gaelic in a
pre-1997 record, but pycountry answers "Guarequena" -- plus a few codes
whose 639-3 scholarly names read oddly on a catalog page (`arc` ->
Aramaic, not "Official Aramaic (700-300 BCE)").

Do not store the display name at ingest time: the code is the
interchange value, it round-trips against `source_marc`, and a stored
name drifts when a cataloger edits the code.

## Testing

Unit tests covering the B/T divergence specifically (`ger`, `fre`,
`dut`, `gre`, `cze`, `per`), the codes this catalog actually uses
(`heb`, `yid`, `lad`, `jrb`, `jpr`, `sam`), the overrides, case and
whitespace normalization, and passthrough for unknown codes. E2e
assertions on record detail and the confirm page, including a German
record -- that is the case a naive fix renders blank.

Also fix `tests/test_views.py:18`, which sets `language="Hebrew"`, a
display name in a code field.

title: source_marc is never populated on records created from a lookup
description:
`Record.source_marc` is meant to hold the archival MARC the record was built from. It is always null: 0 of 11 records have it populated.

`_create_record_from_candidate` sets `source_marc=candidate.get("source_marc")`, but `parse_record` in `sources/marc.py` never emits that key, so the value is `None` on every record the ISBN and title-page paths create.

The field is dead weight in the schema and in the admin, and anything needing to re-derive a value from the original record has nothing to work from.

## Existing rows cannot be backfilled

The source documents were never kept. Fixing the write path does nothing for the records already in the catalog, and there is no local data to recover them from — the only route would be re-fetching each record from NLI, LC or DNB by identifier, which is a separate piece of work and not always possible.

So `source_marc` will be null for the oldest records permanently. Anything built on the field has to tolerate that rather than assuming presence. Accepted deliberately; the point of the fix is that it stops being true for everything created from here on.

## Shape

Have `parse_record` carry the source record through, or have the callers attach it. Prefer whichever keeps the parsed dict serializable, since `candidate_records` is a JSONField and the candidate dict round-trips through the session on the confirm path.

Storing the record verbatim is the point: it is the archival source document, so it should not be cleaned or normalized on the way in. The extraction path is where cleaning belongs.

Check the size cost before committing to it. A MARC record is a few kilobytes, `candidate_records` holds a list of them per scan, and they travel through the session on the confirm path.

title: Score search candidates against the extracted metadata
description:
Candidates come back ordered by source catalog and by each catalog's own relevance, which has no knowledge of the photographed page. A title-only fallback query returns forty editions of Leviticus in arbitrary order, and the reader has to compare each row against the photo by eye. The OCR output is right there and is never used for anything after the query is built.

Score each candidate against the extracted metadata and order by agreement, across catalogs rather than within them.

## Shape

A pure function in `sources/` — `score_candidate(metadata, record)` returning a score and a per-field verdict list — so it is testable without network access and usable from both the cascade view and any later batch tooling. The view sorts by score before rendering; nothing else about the search path changes.

Score over the fields present on both sides, so a sparse catalog record is not punished for what it omits, with a small tiebreaker for the number of fields that agreed. Suggested weights: title heaviest, then author, date, publisher, place. Keep the result in 0..1 so it can be displayed.

Token-set overlap on normalized tokens suits this better than character-ratio fuzzy matching, given Hebrew and romanized forms sitting side by side. `difflib` is enough; no new dependency.

## Per-field normalization

Each field needs its own comparison, and these are the cases this catalog actually produces:

Title — strip MARC display punctuation (` /`, ` :`, ` =`), compare the Hebrew title against the record's title and its 880 alternate, and separately compare the romanized title. Normalize gershayim and geresh against ASCII quotes and apostrophes, strip niqqud.

Author — catalog form is inverted ("Herczeg, Yisrael Isser Zvi"), OCR form is not. Compare as token sets, and check the record's additional authors, not only the first.

Publisher — the same corporate-suffix normalizer that the query builder needs. Build it once and use it in both places.

Place — "Brooklyn, N.Y." against "Brooklyn, New York", plus trailing MARC punctuation.

Date — extract four-digit years from both sides and allow a near miss; catalog dates arrive as `[1999]`, `c1999`, `1994-2003`. A Hebrew year on the title page has no Gregorian form to compare against unless the OCR prompt is asked for both, which is worth doing while the prompt is being reworked for schema-constrained output.

## What the reader sees

The score matters less than the reason for it. Show which fields agreed on each row — title and publisher matched, date did not — so the ordering explains itself and a wrong match is visible rather than hidden behind a number. Never auto-select; the list stays as evidence.

A top score that is very low is also a signal that the query fell through to a broad step, and pairs with surfacing the matched cascade step.

## Testing

Fixtures from real pairs, including a set record matched against a photographed volume, a Hebrew title carrying gershayim, and a record whose only agreement is the publisher.

title: Plan an AWS deployment with S3 backups and a tested restore
description:
Replace the abandoned Fly.io target with an AWS deployment: a deploy that is one push, backups that happen without being remembered, and a restore that has been run rather than described. This ticket is the planning work. What follows is a recommendation for the owner to ratify, with the alternatives costed so a different choice can be made on the same grounds. Implementation is in the child tickets listed at the end; they are written so that only the provisioning ticket changes if the platform does.

## The constraint

The database is one SQLite file at `DATA_DIR/db.sqlite3` in WAL mode (`otzar/settings.py`), and search is an FTS5 virtual table, `catalog_fts`, in the same file (`catalog/search.py`). The index is derived data, rebuilt by `reindex_all()`, but it travels with the file: any file-level copy carries it. One writer, on a local disk, in one process. That rules out anything that treats the filesystem as ephemeral (App Runner, Lightsail's container service), anything that runs more than one instance, and network filesystems: SQLite's own documentation says NFS locking is unreliable, EFS users report stale locks and corruption under concurrent access, every lock and fsync becomes a network round trip, and Litestream also wants a local file. Fargate with EFS is therefore ruled out on evidence, not preference. What remains is one small always-on machine with a disk that persists, which is what the container was written for.

## Recommendation

Lightsail, the 1 GB / 2 vCPU / 40 GB dual-stack Linux bundle, Ubuntu 24.04, Docker and Caddy on the instance, in the region nearest the users. Two S3 buckets in the same region: media (versioned, served through presigned URLs) and backups (Litestream replica plus dated snapshots). Media goes to S3 through Django's storage API. Deploy is a push to `main`: CI builds the image, pushes it to GHCR, and restarts the container over SSH. Restore is rehearsed on a throwaway instance and the result written down. About $8 to $9 a month.

## Compute, costed

On-demand list prices, us-east-1, September 2026.

- Lightsail 1 GB bundle: $7/month, includes 2 vCPU, 40 GB SSD, 2 TB transfer, a static IPv4 and the firewall. Automatic daily snapshots (seven kept) at $0.05 per GB-month, roughly $0.50 at this disk's fill. The 2 GB bundle is $12.
- EC2 t4g.micro (1 GB, Graviton): $6.13/month, plus gp3 20 GB $1.60, plus the public IPv4 charge $3.65, plus EBS snapshots about $0.50: about $12. t4g.small (2 GB): about $18. A one-year savings plan takes roughly a third off the instance line; not worth committing to before the first deploy.
- Fargate 0.25 vCPU / 0.5 GB: about $9/month for the task, plus IPv4 $3.65, plus EFS, plus either an ALB (about $16) or a task IP that changes on every deploy. Ruled out above on SQLite grounds regardless of price.
- App Runner: no persistent disk. Ruled out unless the database leaves SQLite, which is out of scope.
- Common to every option: S3 under $1/month at this catalog's size (storage $0.023/GB-month; Litestream's request volume at the 1 s sync interval is a few thousand PUTs a month of light cataloging at $0.005 per thousand); GHCR and Actions free on a public repository; DNS free at the registrar or $0.50 for a Route 53 zone; Caddy and Let's Encrypt free. The free tier is not planned around: accounts created since July 2025 get credits rather than free instance hours, and Lightsail's three-month trial applies to the paid plan only.

What drives the cost is the always-on instance, which the single-writer design requires, and the IPv4 address (bundled in Lightsail, $3.65 on EC2). Storage and S3 do not register.

Why Lightsail over EC2: it is $4 to $6 a month cheaper for the same memory once IPv4 and the disk are counted; there is nothing to design (no VPC, security group, EBS volume, AMI or role: the bundle is machine, disk, IP, firewall and snapshots); it is the closest analogue to the Fly machine and volume the container was written against; and Lightsail can export an instance to EC2 if the needs grow. What EC2 would buy, for the owner to weigh: an instance role, so no static access key sits on the box (Lightsail cannot attach one, so Litestream and the media backend authenticate with a key for an IAM user scoped to the two buckets, kept in the instance's `.env`, rotated by hand); Graviton, which is cheaper per unit of work but irrelevant at this load; resizing in place with a stop and start, where Lightsail needs a snapshot and a relaunch; and CloudWatch integration. If the owner values the instance role more than $5 a month and a shorter provisioning script, choose t4g.micro; only the provisioning ticket changes.

Memory: 1 GB is enough. OS and Docker about 250 MB, Caddy 30 MB, two gunicorn workers about 250 MB, Litestream 30 MB; image builds happen in CI, not on the box; the browser resizes photos to 1500 px before upload so Pillow's peak is small. Add a 1 GB swap file. If `free -m` shows swap in steady use, snapshot and relaunch on the 2 GB bundle.

## Media

`media/` holds staged title-page photos and, after bd-yg9, the photos attached to records: large, append-mostly, no transactional consistency needed. Two workable answers. On the instance disk, served by Caddy, synced hourly to a versioned bucket: no new dependency, dev and production identical, but the disk becomes a second system of record, restore has a second step, and the machine is stateful in two places. On S3 through `django-storages`, switched on by an environment variable: the machine then holds only the database, which Litestream already streams, so machine loss costs nothing in media and the restore is one mechanism; bucket versioning is the media backup; the disk never fills. The costs are a dependency (`django-storages` and `boto3`), a code path CI does not run (covered by a post-deploy smoke test that uploads a photo), and on Lightsail the static key. The code already goes through the storage API everywhere (`scan.image.open`, `scan.image.delete`, `.url`; nothing reads `.path`), so the change is settings, not application code. Recommendation: S3. Whichever is chosen, it has to be chosen before the first deploy: `otzar/urls.py` serves `/media/` only when `DEBUG` is true, so production today serves no images at all.

## Backups

Two mechanisms, because they protect against different things.

Continuous replication, Litestream in the container image, replica at `s3://<backup bucket>/litestream/db`, sync interval 1 s, snapshot every 24 h, retention 168 h. Losing the machine loses at most the last second of writes, and any moment in the last seven days is restorable with `-timestamp`. The default retention of 24 h is too short to be useful for a mistake noticed the next day, so it is raised.

Dated snapshots, a management command run daily by a host timer and by the deploy script before every deploy: `sqlite3.Connection.backup()` (the online-backup API, safe against a live WAL database) to a temporary file, gzipped, uploaded to `snapshots/YYYY/MM/DD/` with a manifest holding the record count and the commit; copied to `monthly/` on the first of the month. Lifecycle rules expire `snapshots/` after 35 days and `monthly/` after 400. These are self-contained SQLite files anyone can download and open with `sqlite3`, with no dependence on Litestream's format or on knowing when the damage happened. A bad migration or a mistaken bulk edit is undone from the pre-deploy snapshot or from the day before.

What retention buys is the maximum delay between a mistake and noticing it: seven days to the second, 35 days to the day, 13 months to the month. The whole of it costs cents.

Media: bucket versioning with noncurrent versions expiring after 30 days. Instance snapshots (daily, seven kept) roll back the machine itself, not the catalog. Not backed up, deliberately: `DATA_DIR/cache` (derived) and `staticfiles` (in the image).

## Restore

Executed on a throwaway instance launched by the same provisioning script, with replication switched off and a read-only IAM key so the drill cannot write into the production replica or the media bucket. Both paths are run: `litestream restore` (latest and `-timestamp`) and a snapshot file gunzipped into place. Verification, each value recorded: `Record.objects.count()` equals the manifest's or production's count read before the restore; one record chosen at drill time has the same title, authors and identifiers; a search on a word from that title returns it, with `manage.py reindex` run and noted if it does not, since the FTS table and its shadow tables are in the same file and should not need it; the record's image returns 200; `/health/` returns 200 through Caddy. The date, commit, snapshot, counts and outcome are written into `docs/administration.md`, and the drill is repeated after any change to the backup path and otherwise quarterly.

## Deploy

One push. Merging to `main` triggers a workflow after CI succeeds: build the image (`linux/amd64` for Lightsail; `linux/arm64` on GitHub's free ARM runner if the host is Graviton), push `ghcr.io/dchud/otzar:<sha>`, SSH to the instance, run `deploy.sh`: pre-deploy snapshot, `docker compose pull`, `docker compose up -d`, wait for `/health/`, print backup freshness. Migrations run automatically in the entrypoint as they do today; the pre-deploy snapshot is the rollback point. Secrets: the instance's `/opt/otzar/.env` (root, 0600) holds every application secret and the bucket key, written by hand once; GitHub holds only the deploy SSH key and the host. Parameter Store with an instance role is the EC2 variant; Secrets Manager's per-secret charge buys nothing here. `just deploy [sha]` is the manual equivalent for emergencies and the drill. The entrypoint refuses to start when `DATA_DIR` is unset or is `/app`, because an unset `DATA_DIR` silently runs against the image's own filesystem and the next deploy discards the catalog.

## Out of scope

Moving off SQLite: a large change with its own tradeoffs, not to be smuggled in through deployment. Multiple catalogs on one host (long-term plan section 6). A CDN, an alerting system beyond the freshness ages the deploy and the drill print, and any second instance.

## Findings the brief did not anticipate

- Production serves no media today; the media decision precedes the first deploy.
- Django's default logging drops production errors: the console handler is DEBUG-only and request errors go to an unconfigured `mail_admins`. `check --deploy` also reports the proxy header and secure-cookie settings unset, and gunicorn's `--forwarded-allow-ips` must name the Docker bridge, not `127.0.0.1`, when Caddy is on the host. One settings ticket covers these and is platform-neutral.
- The Dockerfile's `DATABASE_URL` line is dead: settings read `DATA_DIR`. `collectstatic` does not open the database, so the build is unaffected, but the runtime guard above matters.
- Lightsail has no instance roles; this is the one security tradeoff of the recommendation.
- Litestream 0.5 defaults to 24 h retention.
- A drill instance running the production entrypoint would replicate into the production replica path; the entrypoint needs an off switch.
- `docs/deployment.md` has been empty since bd-mej; the deploy ticket writes it.
- PR #39 (stylesheet built in the image) and PR #37 (`manage.py reindex`) have both merged: the image needs nothing from the deploy, and the drill has a command for rebuilding the index.
- The `AWS_*` placeholders in `.env.example` become live in the media and Litestream tickets and their "no code reads these" note goes.

## Implementation tickets

In order. bd-n7a.1 and bd-n7a.2 are application changes that can be done now and hold on any platform; bd-n7a.3 is the image and holds on any Docker host; bd-n7a.4 is the only platform-specific ticket; bd-n7a.5 needs the four before it; bd-n7a.6 needs bd-n7a.5.

1. bd-n7a.1: production settings behind a TLS-terminating proxy.
2. bd-n7a.2: media in S3 through a storage backend selected by environment.
3. bd-n7a.3: Litestream replication and daily snapshots in the image.
4. bd-n7a.4: provision the Lightsail instance, buckets and IAM user with a script.
5. bd-n7a.5: deploy on push to main through GHCR and SSH.
6. bd-n7a.6: run a restore onto a throwaway instance and record the result.

title: Render language codes as language names
description:
Language shows as the raw code -- `heb` rather than `Hebrew` -- on the
record detail page, the ingest confirm page, the scan poll partial, the
manual entry form, and in the admin filter.

## The trap

MARC 008/35-37 carries ISO 639-2/**B** bibliographic codes, so German is
`ger`, not `deu`. `sources/marc.py:197` reads exactly those bytes, and
`catalog/language_views.py:19` already stores the bibliographic form.

`pycountry` (already a dependency) indexes ISO 639-3, where these exist
only as a `bibliographic` alias:

    pycountry.languages.get(alpha_3="ger")       -> None
    pycountry.languages.get(bibliographic="ger") -> German

An alpha_3-only lookup renders German, French, Dutch, Greek, Czech,
Persian, Chinese, Romanian, Welsh, Basque, Armenian, Icelandic,
Georgian, Macedonian, Maori, Malay, Burmese, Slovak, Albanian and
Tibetan as blank -- 20 divergences. Bibliographic lookup must come
first.

## Shape

A plain module `catalog/language_codes.py` plus a template filter
library, following the existing `bidi` templatetag pattern. Shared
rather than living inside the templatetag because
`catalog/language_views.py` is a second consumer.

Two display sites render plain dicts from session/JSON rather than model
instances, so this has to be a filter, not a model property.

A small override table is needed for MARC codes withdrawn from ISO 639-2
that ISO 639-3 has since reassigned -- `gae` means Scottish Gaelic in a
pre-1997 record, but pycountry answers "Guarequena" -- plus a few codes
whose 639-3 scholarly names read oddly on a catalog page (`arc` ->
Aramaic, not "Official Aramaic (700-300 BCE)").

Do not store the display name at ingest time: the code is the
interchange value, it round-trips against `source_marc`, and a stored
name drifts when a cataloger edits the code.

## Testing

Unit tests covering the B/T divergence specifically (`ger`, `fre`,
`dut`, `gre`, `cze`, `per`), the codes this catalog actually uses
(`heb`, `yid`, `lad`, `jrb`, `jpr`, `sam`), the overrides, case and
whitespace normalization, and passthrough for unknown codes. E2e
assertions on record detail and the confirm page, including a German
record -- that is the case a naive fix renders blank.

Also fix `tests/test_views.py:18`, which sets `language="Hebrew"`, a
display name in a code field.

title: A failed FTS rebuild leaves the index empty and never repairs it
description:
`ensure_fts_table` decides whether to rebuild by comparing the table's columns to `FTS_COLUMNS`. Rebuilding is two steps — `rebuild_fts_table()` drops and recreates the table, then `_index_all_records()` fills it — and nothing makes them atomic.

If the second step fails, the table is left with the correct shape and no rows. Every later call compares columns, finds them matching, and returns without repopulating. Search then returns nothing, for every query, permanently, with no error.

## Reproduced

Hit on the live catalog immediately after PR #28 merged. The code was current but `catalog.0005_record_provenance` had not been applied yet, so:

1. `ensure_fts_table()` saw a 10-column table, dropped it, recreated it with 11 columns.
2. `_index_all_records()` raised `OperationalError: no such column: catalog_record.provenance`.
3. The next call saw 11 columns matching `FTS_COLUMNS` and returned immediately.
4. `search_records("Piano")` returned 0 hits where it had returned 1. The index held 0 rows against 11 records.

`reindex_all()` restored it, but nothing would have prompted anyone to run it — the failure is silent and looks like an empty catalog.

## Why it matters beyond the migration case

The migration-ordering trigger is unlikely in production, since `entrypoint.sh` migrates before starting gunicorn. But any interruption between the two steps produces the same state: a process killed mid-reindex, a deploy restarting the container, an exception on one malformed record. The index is derived data, so the cost is recoverable — but only by someone who notices, and a search returning nothing looks like a catalog problem rather than an index problem.

## Shape

Make the rebuild recoverable rather than assuming it completes. Options worth weighing: do the drop, recreate and repopulate in one transaction so a failure rolls back to the old table; or have the emptiness itself be detectable, so a table whose shape is right but whose row count is zero while records exist gets repopulated rather than trusted.

Prefer whichever keeps `ensure_fts_table` cheap — it is called on the path of every search, so it must not count rows against the record table on every query.

Worth checking whether `index_record` failing for one record during a rebuild should abort the whole thing or skip that record and report.

Found while verifying PR #28 against the live catalog.

title: Rework the review queue into scannable rows with inline confirm

Details button at the far right of each row. Deciding whether a scan

then offers "Use this" with little more to go on.

`_candidates.html` -- written for the title-page cascade results --
already renders the layout this needs: title/author, date,
publisher/place, series, identifiers, source, one row per candidate.
The queue's `_queue_item.html` predates it and duplicates none of it.

button inside the expanded row, so the decision and the action sit

title-page results reach, so the queue stops being the one path that

title: A failed OCR re-run discards the previous extraction
description:
`run_ocr` accepts `pending` scans so the user can re-run against the
same image. On `metadata is None` it sets `ocr_output = None` and
reverts status to `awaiting_ocr` unconditionally.

So: the user has usable metadata on screen, presses "Re-run OCR" hoping
for a better read, the vision call fails transiently or returns
unparseable JSON, and the extraction they already had is gone. The edit
form is replaced by the error partial and there is no way back to it.

This is current intended behaviour --
`test_run_ocr_failure_after_success_resets_to_awaiting` asserts it, with
the rationale that the queue card should surface the scan again. The
question is whether that rationale outweighs destroying a good result on
a transient failure.

Suggested: only overwrite `ocr_output` on success, and leave a scan that
was already `pending` in `pending`. The failure notice can offer both
"Try again" and "Keep the previous result". That test would change to
assert the previous output survives.

Found in review of PR #7. Needs a decision before implementing, since it
reverses a deliberate choice.

title: Title-page scans never leave pending after a candidate is chosen
description:
Photograph a title page, run OCR, search catalogs, pick a candidate: a
Record is created and the ScanResult stays `status="pending"` with
`ocr_output` set, forever.

`title_page_poll` shows `pending` rows that have output, so the card
reappears in the "Incoming photos" pane on every device on every poll
tick, and sits in `/ingest/queue/` permanently. The pane fills with
scans that are already catalogued.

The link is dropped in the round trip. `_ocr_results.html`'s search form
posts only the metadata fields to `title_page_upload`; the response,
`_candidates.html`, has a "Use" button that posts to `select_candidate`
-> `confirm_candidate`. Nothing in that chain knows which ScanResult the
metadata came from, so nothing can mark it confirmed.

Carry `scan.id` through the search form and the candidate form, and set
`status="confirmed"`, `created_record`, and
`selected_candidate_index` when the record is created --
`confirm_scan` already does exactly this for the queue path.

Found in review of PR #7. P1 because every successful title-page ingest
leaves permanent debris in the one pane the workflow depends on.

title: Staged images keep a .png suffix over JPEG bytes
description:
`staging_image_path` in `ingest/models.py` allows `.png` through
`JPEG_SUFFIXES`, but the capture form re-encodes every selection to
`image/jpeg` while preserving the original filename.

Pick a PNG screenshot of a title page and it is stored at
`staging/.../<hex>.png` holding JPEG bytes, and served as
`Content-Type: image/png`. Browsers sniff past it; anything trusting the
extension or MIME type does not.

Given the unconditional re-encode, the suffix should normalise to `.jpg`
for anything that is not already `.jpg`/`.jpeg`. The docstring already
explains the re-encode, so this is a one-line change plus a test.

Found in review of PR #7.

title: Keep subject subdivisions and dedupe repeated headings
description:
The ingest confirm page shows the same subject twice.

`sources/marc.py:210-216` keeps only the first `$a` of each 650 field
and discards the subdivisions (`$v $x $y $z`), with no deduplication.
That produces visually identical entries two ways, both routine:

- Subdivided headings collapse. `650 _0 $a Jews $z Israel $x History.`
  and `650 _0 $a Jews $x Social life and customs.` both emit `Jews`.
- Parallel vocabularies repeat. LC records carry an LCSH `650 _0 $a
  Judaism.` alongside a FAST `650 _7 $a Judaism. $2 fast`; the `$2` is
  invisible here, so the list holds the heading twice.

Reproduced against a synthetic LC-shaped record: five 650 fields yielded
`['Jews', 'Jews', 'Judaism.', 'Judaism.', 'Jews']`.

The visible duplication is display-only -- `get_or_create(heading=...)`
collapses equal headings and the through table has a unique index, so no
duplicate rows exist. The real defect is underneath it: two distinct
headings are both stored as the broad subject `Jews`. The intended form
joins subdivisions with " -- ", as `load_test_data.py:284-289` shows
("Talmud -- Commentaries").

Fix by assembling the heading from `$a` plus subdivisions and deduping
on a normalized key, in `sources/marc.py`. `_attach_from_candidate` is
the single writer for all three ingest paths, so one fix covers
everything. Deduping in the template would hide the symptom and keep
storing the wrong subject.

Existing tests stay green (`tests/test_marc.py:282-284` covers 650s that
carry only `$a`). Add a case with a subdivided 650 plus a duplicate FAST
650, and an e2e assertion that the confirm page lists each subject once.

The 8 existing Subject rows were written under the truncating logic; a
backfill would need the original MARC, and no stored record has
`source_marc` populated yet.

title: Populate romanized subject and series headings from linked 880 fields
description:
`Subject.heading_romanized` and `Series.title_romanized` exist and nothing fills them. `parse_record` in `sources/marc.py` resolves 880 linkage only for 245 (title) and 100 (author) through `_linked_880_value`; the 650 subject loop and the 490/830 series extraction read the primary field alone. An LC record for a Hebrew book therefore yields romanized subjects with no Hebrew form, an NLI record yields Hebrew subjects with no romanized form, and the subject browse page shows one heading twice in two scripts from two sources.

Extend the 650 and 490/830 extraction to return the linked 880 value as an alternate, carry it on the candidate dict, and store it on confirm in `_attach_from_candidate` and the series persistence path. Matching a subject or series by either script form belongs with this change so the two forms merge into one row; the subject deduplication that landed with subdivision handling is the place to add it, and `find_matching_series` the place for series.

title: Add a DNB cascade to the title-page search
description:
`run_cascade` in `sources/cascade.py` runs the NLI and LC step lists; DNB is queried only in `isbn_lookup`. A title-page photograph of a German or Yiddish book reaches two catalogs that hold little of that material and skips the one that does. The cascade is data: a `DNB_CASCADE` list of `(name, CQL template)` pairs in DNB's index vocabulary, and a `search_dnb` wrapper, make it a third source rendered by the same candidate partial. Confirm the index names against DNB's SRU explain response before writing the templates.

Worth doing when a DNB-held book fails the title-page path. The one DNB record in the catalog arrived through ISBN.

title: Constrain OCR output with a response schema
description:
`extract_metadata_from_image` asks for JSON in the prompt text and then repairs whatever comes back. `_parse_vision_json` strips markdown fences, and when parsing fails it rewrites any double quote sitting between two Hebrew characters as a gershayim (U+05F4) and tries again. A quote that lands anywhere else — beside a Latin letter, a digit, a space, or punctuation — still fails, `extract_metadata_from_image` returns None, and the user sees "OCR could not extract metadata" for a photo the model read correctly.

Hebrew title pages carry gershayim constantly (רש״י, תשע״ד), so this is a routine failure, not an edge case.

Structured outputs remove the failure class: constrain the response to a JSON schema covering the eight metadata keys. The fence stripping, the gershayim repair, and the None-on-unparseable path all go away, and a genuine extraction failure becomes distinguishable from a serialization accident. Check the current API shape against the `claude-api` skill rather than writing the request from memory.

The remaining model-id cleanup is in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, which sets `CLAUDE_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` in two places. Current ids are unsuffixed.

`ingest/ocr.py` and `.env.example` no longer need attention: the default is already `claude-sonnet-5` and the per-scan costs were refreshed alongside it.

title: A failed OCR re-run discards the previous extraction
description:
`run_ocr` accepts `pending` scans so the user can re-run against the
same image. On `metadata is None` it sets `ocr_output = None` and
reverts status to `awaiting_ocr` unconditionally.

So: the user has usable metadata on screen, presses "Re-run OCR" hoping
for a better read, the vision call fails transiently or returns
unparseable JSON, and the extraction they already had is gone. The edit
form is replaced by the error partial and there is no way back to it.

This is current intended behaviour --
`test_run_ocr_failure_after_success_resets_to_awaiting` asserts it, with
the rationale that the queue card should surface the scan again. The
question is whether that rationale outweighs destroying a good result on
a transient failure.

Suggested: only overwrite `ocr_output` on success, and leave a scan that
was already `pending` in `pending`. The failure notice can offer both
"Try again" and "Keep the previous result". That test would change to
assert the previous output survives.

Found in review of PR #7. Needs a decision before implementing, since it
reverses a deliberate choice.

title: Connect the response cache, API usage log and search reindex paths
description:
Three pieces of infrastructure exist with unit tests and nothing calls them: `ResponseCache` in `sources/cache.py` (a 30-day file cache keyed on URL and parameters), `APIUsageLog` in `ingest/models.py` (an OCR cost table with an admin page and no writers), and `reindex_all` in `catalog/search.py` (invoked only by `load_test_data`). A fourth gap sits beside them: records edited or deleted through the Django admin bypass `index_record`, so the FTS index goes stale with no signal.

Each child is small and independent of the others. Together they connect parts of the system that are written but not running.

title: Wire ResponseCache into the SRU and VIAF clients
description:
`SRUClient.search` in `sources/sru.py` sleeps for the polite delay and calls `httpx.get` on every invocation. `ResponseCache` in `sources/cache.py` offers `get(base_url, params)` and `set(...)` over Django's file cache with a 30-day TTL, and nothing calls it. A repeated title-page search replays every cascade step against NLI and LC with a three-second delay per step, so re-running a search that already ran costs twenty seconds or more and the same load on the source catalogs.

Check the cache before the delay and the request; store the raw XML on success only, so a transient failure is retried rather than remembered. Apply the same to `sources/viaf.py`. The cache directory is `DATA_DIR/cache`, already configured. Add tests that a second identical `search` call makes no HTTP request; pytest-socket blocks the network in tests, so the assertion is that the cached call succeeds where an uncached one raises.

The series claim work fans out one search per volume; with caching, a retried or reopened claim costs nothing at the source catalogs.
close_reason: Merged in PR #41

title: Add a reindex management command and index records saved through the admin
description:
`index_record` is called from the ingest views when a record is created or edited, and from nowhere else. `RecordAdmin` in `catalog/admin.py` has no `save_model` or `delete_model` override and no signal handler exists, so a record edited in the admin keeps its old text in the FTS index and one deleted in the admin leaves an orphaned index row. Author, subject and publisher text is denormalized into the index, so renaming an author in the admin leaves every one of that author's records stale too. `reindex_all` exists in `catalog/search.py` and only `load_test_data` calls it; an operator has no command to recover with.

Two parts. A `reindex` management command that calls `ensure_fts_table` and `reindex_all` and reports a count. And index maintenance on admin writes: either `post_save`/`post_delete` handlers on `Record`, on its M2M through tables and on the related models (so a renamed author reindexes its records), or explicit `save_model`/`delete_model` overrides on each ModelAdmin. Handlers cover every write path including future ones; overrides are explicit and easier to read. Pick one and apply it to every model the index reads from.

Tests: edit a record through the admin client and search for the new title; delete through the admin and confirm the index row is gone; run the command against a database with a dropped FTS table and confirm every record is searchable afterwards.

title: Log OCR calls to APIUsageLog and enforce a daily scan limit
description:
`APIUsageLog` in `ingest/models.py` has fields for api, model, user and input and output tokens, a migration and an admin page, and no code writes to it. `extract_metadata` in `ingest/ocr.py` receives the Anthropic `message` object, whose `usage` carries the token counts, and discards it. The admin page for OCR cost is therefore always empty, and nothing limits how many scans a user or a day can run.

Write one row per OCR call from `run_ocr`, which knows the user and the scan, with the model name, token counts and whether the call produced a reading. `extract_metadata` returns only the parsed dict, so either return the usage alongside it or log from inside the function with the caller passing the user. Add a configurable daily cap on OCR calls (an env var with a generous default) that `run_ocr` checks before calling the API and names in the failure partial when exceeded, so a retry loop on a phone cannot spend without bound.

title: Compress HTTP responses
description:
`GZipMiddleware` is not in `MIDDLEWARE`, so no dynamic response is compressed. Whitenoise compresses static files only.

This matters more than it usually would because the heaviest pages are the ones a phone loads. The ingest workflow is explicitly phone-first — the phone is the camera, and the candidate list is reviewed on it — and cataloging happens at the shelves, where wifi is unreliable.

Concrete numbers, measured against a real 20-record NLI response while adding `source_marc` to candidates: the candidate results page is about 111 KB uncompressed and 15.3 KB gzipped. An ISBN lookup that hits NLI, LC and DNB at `max_records=20` could reach roughly 300 KB. Compression removes about 85% of that for one line of configuration.

## Shape

Add `django.middleware.gzip.GZipMiddleware` near the top of `MIDDLEWARE`, above the middleware whose output it should compress and in the position Django's documentation specifies.

Read the security note before doing it. Django's docs warn about the BREACH attack when compressing responses that contain both a CSRF token and attacker-controlled content. Django mitigates this by masking CSRF tokens per response, so the standard advice is that enabling it is safe, but the reasoning should be understood and stated rather than assumed. If it is not safe here, say why and close this rather than shipping it quietly.

Check whether anything downstream would double-compress once a real deployment exists (bd-n7a). A reverse proxy compressing an already-compressed response wastes work.
close_reason: Merged in PR #38

title: Attach the confirmed title-page image to the record and show it on the record page
description:
A title-page scan stores its photo on `ScanResult.image` under `media/staging/YYYY/MM/DD/`. Confirming the scan creates the Record through `_create_record_from_candidate` and leaves the image on the ScanResult; nothing moves it. `TitlePageImage` in `catalog/models.py` has a model with `upload_to="title-pages/%Y/%m/%d/"` and a `staged` flag, a migration and an admin inline, and no code creates one. So the photograph that identified the book stays a staging artifact instead of becoming part of the record. For a collection of old books, where the title page is the identity of the copy, that is the wrong outcome.

On confirm of an OCR scan, create a `TitlePageImage` for the new Record, move the file from staging to its permanent path through Django's storage API (so the code does not change if media moves to S3 under bd-n7a), set `staged=False`, and clear `ScanResult.image`. Show the image on the record page below the cover. The manual entry and edit form can gain an upload field for the same model afterwards; this ticket covers the scan path. E2e: confirm a title-page scan and see the image on the record page.

title: Persist the title-statement fields when a candidate is confirmed
description:
The parser reads 245 `$n`, `$p` and `$c` and the `Record` model has `volume_part_number`, `volume_part_title` and `statement_of_responsibility`, but nothing writes them: `_create_record_from_candidate` was left untouched because another change owned `ingest/views.py` at the time. So the values show on candidate cards and are dropped the moment a record is created.

This is the remaining half of otzar-cex and the first half of otzar-55i.

## Shape

Three assignments on the `Record(...)` constructor in `_create_record_from_candidate`:

    volume_part_number=strip_marc_punctuation(candidate.get("volume_part_number")),
    volume_part_title=strip_marc_punctuation(candidate.get("volume_part_title")),
    statement_of_responsibility=strip_marc_punctuation(candidate.get("statement_of_responsibility")),

That one function serves both confirm entry points, `confirm_candidate` and `confirm_scan`, so there is nowhere else to change.

`strip_marc_punctuation` is load-bearing rather than cosmetic. The record page supplies its own ISBD colon between the part number and the part title, which assumes the stored values arrive without the cataloger's transcribed punctuation. Candidate dicts deliberately keep that punctuation; saved records deliberately do not.

## Testing

A unit test in `tests/test_ingest.py` asserting the three fields survive a confirm, and an e2e case that confirms a candidate and finds the values on the resulting record page.

## Not in scope

The role column on the record-author link populated from `700$e`/`$4` — the second half of otzar-55i, which needs its own relator-code mapping. And parsing roles out of `$c` prose, which otzar-55i rules out explicitly.

title: Per-user activity view of records cataloged in a session
description: A cataloger working through a shelf has no page that answers "what did I add today?" `Record.created_by` and `ScanResult.scanned_by` hold the data, `created_at` the times. A page under `/ingest/` listing the current user's records and scans grouped by day, newest first, with counts, gives a work session a visible result and a place to catch a mistaken confirm while it is fresh. Public browse pages stay as they are; this is a logged-in view.

title: Live phone-to-laptop barcode scanning flow
description:
When scanning barcodes on the phone via QR handoff, results should appear on the laptop in real-time instead of on the phone.

Current flow: phone scans barcode → results show on phone → confirm on phone.
Target flow: phone scans barcode → ScanResult created → laptop sees it immediately → confirm on laptop.

Implementation:

1. Phone scan page behavior change: after ISBN lookup returns candidates, create a ScanResult (scan_type='isbn') and show a simple 'Sent to review queue' confirmation instead of rendering candidates on the phone. Phone stays ready for the next scan.

2. Laptop scan page live updates: add an HTMX polling region (hx-trigger='every 3s') that checks for new pending ScanResults for the current user. When a new one arrives, render candidates inline on the scan page so the user can confirm/discard without navigating to the review queue.

3. The QR token already encodes the user PK, so phone scans are attributed to the correct user via the ScanResult.scanned_by FK. No session/pairing ID needed beyond what exists.

4. After confirming a candidate on the laptop, the poll area resets to 'waiting for scans' and the phone can scan the next book.

5. Consider: should the phone auto-restart the camera after sending a scan? This would allow rapid scanning of multiple books.

Technical approach:
- New HTMX partial endpoint: GET /ingest/scan/poll/ returns pending ScanResults for current user as HTML fragment
- Laptop scan page includes a div with hx-get pointing to that endpoint, hx-trigger='every 3s'
- Phone scan page: detect if arrived via QR (e.g. session flag set by phone_scan_auth) and switch to 'scanner mode' — auto-submit to queue instead of rendering candidates
- Confirm/discard actions on the laptop post back and the poll refreshes

No new dependencies needed — HTMX polling is built in.

title: Enrich author and subject records from authority sources
description:
Explore options for enhancing catalog metadata using external authority sources:

Authors:
- Wikidata: biographical info, dates, alternate names, links to Wikipedia articles
- LC Name Authority File (id.loc.gov): authorized forms, cross-references
- VIAF: already partially integrated for variant names; could pull more data (associated works, dates)
- NLI J9U authority records

- Could enable hierarchical subject browsing (e.g., 'Jewish law' → 'Talmud' → 'Bava Metzia')

title: Offer existing author matches when confirming a scan
description:
`_create_record_from_candidate` in `ingest/views.py` creates authors with `Author.objects.get_or_create(name=author_name)`, and `_attach_from_candidate` does the same for additional authors. The same person arrives as `שניאור זלמן מלאדי` from NLI and `Shneur Zalman, of Lyady` from LC, so confirming two editions from two catalogs yields two Author rows, and the author browse page lists them apart. Every confirm through the ISBN path, the title-page path and the review queue takes this route, and nothing merges rows afterwards. This is the largest data-quality gap in the catalog and it compounds with every confirm.

`find_author_matches` in `ingest/authority.py` matches a name against existing authors by exact name, exact romanized name, or normalized variant-name form, and is called only from the `authority_check` endpoint the manual entry form uses. Call it in the confirm path with both the candidate's `author` and `author_alternate`; when it finds one strong match, attach that Author instead of creating one. When the match is ambiguous (several hits, or a hit by variant only) show a choice on the confirm page rather than picking silently; the queue's inline confirm can default to the strongest match and say which it chose.

When the candidate carries an alternate-script author form from an 880 field, store it on the Author row (`name_romanized` when the primary is Hebrew, `variant_names` otherwise) so later matches across scripts have something to hit. This is the local step; matching through VIAF identifiers is the parent ticket.

title: Auto-extract all MARC fields on record creation from catalog lookup
description:
When a record is created via ISBN lookup or OCR cascade (selecting a candidate), the full MARC record data should be extracted and saved to all related models — not just the few fields that go through the manual entry form.

Current problem: the ISBN lookup flow passes a handful of fields as GET params to the manual entry form. This loses: additional authors, subjects, series info, all external identifiers (LCCN, OCLC, etc.), the source MARC record itself, and the publication date from the 008 field.

Fix: when a candidate is selected (either from ISBN lookup _candidates.html or OCR results), the full parsed record data should be stored (e.g. in the session) and used to populate all related models on save. Specifically:

1. Store the full parsed record dict AND the raw marcjson in the session when a candidate is selected
2. On manual_entry form save, if session has candidate data:
   - Save source_marc (marcjson) and source_catalog on the Record
   - Extract and create ALL authors (not just the first) from MARC 100 and 700 fields
   - Extract and create subjects from MARC 650 fields
   - Extract publication date from MARC 008 or 260/264
   - Extract and save external identifiers (LCCN from 010, OCLC from 035, ISBN from 020)
   - Extract series info from 490/830
3. The manual entry form still allows the user to review and override, but defaults come from the MARC data

Files to modify:
- ingest/views.py (isbn_lookup_view, manual_entry)
- ingest/templates/ingest/_candidates.html (pass full parsed data, not just a few fields)
- sources/marc.py (may need to extract 700 additional authors, 010 LCCN, 035 OCLC)
